blocks.passage:
Every year, businesses lose money to fraud. The most common problem is simple: a seller ships goods to a buyer who never really existed, or who never planned to pay.

This is where due diligence comes in. Before you do business with a new partner, you should check who they are. Look up the company. Ask for references. Run a basic background check. Visit them, if you can.

A few quiet questions at the start save a lot of pain at the end.

items.why: "a seller ships goods to a buyer who never really existed, or who never planned to pay."

options: Because it filters out fake or non-paying buyers before you lose money

audio.text:
Before we approve any new supplier, we always run three basic checks. They're quick, and they save us from most fraud. Let me walk you through them.

Check one: does the company really exist? We look them up in the official company register. If we can't find them, that's a big red flag. A real business is on the record.

Check two: what do others say? We ask for references — two or three other companies who have worked with them. Then we actually call those references. A fraudster usually can't give real ones.

Check three: a quick search online. We look for the company name and the owner's name. We're checking for bad news — court cases, fraud stories, angry customers.

If all three come back fine, we go ahead, but we still start small — a smaller first order, payment secured. If anything looks strange, we slow down and ask more questions.

None of this is complicated. It's just three quiet questions before we trust someone with our goods. Careful at the start, calm at the end.
